title: The Promise None of Them Kept
excerpt: Promise theory described agents that observe, reason, and commit. The IaC generation never delivered it and CFEngine came closest. LLMs supplied the missing reasoning layer, and swamp is built for the agent that has it.
content_html:
Mark Burgess shipped CFEngine in 1993, formalized promise theory with Siri Fagernes around 2005, and published In Search of Certainty in 2015. The model is precise: autonomous agents observe their environment, reason locally about what they find, and make promises about their own behavior. The agent does not receive instructions from a controller. The agent looks around, decides what to do, and commits to doing it.

Every infrastructure tool since has claimed some lineage from this idea. Chef called its resources “convergent.” Puppet called its catalogs “desired state.” Terraform called its plans “declarative.” Ansible called its playbooks “idempotent.”

None of those four kept the promise. Burgess’s own tool did, and ran into a different limit.

The reason to revisit any of this now is that the missing piece finally shipped, and it arrived from outside infrastructure entirely. LLMs supply the reasoning layer promise theory always assumed: an agent can observe a live system, weigh what it finds against context nobody enumerated in advance, and decide whether to act. Four generations of tooling could not do that at any price. CFEngine came closest and stopped short for reasons worth being precise about, and swamp is built for the agent that can.

The promise theory control loop

Promise theory starts from three axioms. An agent is autonomous and cannot be coerced. An agent can only promise its own behavior. An agent’s knowledge of the world is local. Compose them and you get a control loop:

  1. Observation. The agent perceives its environment directly. Not from a file. Not from a state snapshot someone else produced. The agent looks. Knowledge is local, so no global observer exists to hand the agent a summary, and a promise is assessed by whoever observes it, so an assessment the agent did not make itself buys it nothing.

  2. Local reasoning. The agent decides what to do based on what it observed. No central controller dictates the action. The agent’s judgment is sovereign within its domain.

  3. Voluntary commitment. The agent promises its own behavior. It does not impose behavior on others. A promise is a commitment you make about yourself, never an obligation you push onto a remote system. An imposition the receiving agent never promised to accept accomplishes nothing.

Observe, reason, commit. The loop leaves out most of promise theory, including trust accumulation, cooperative equilibria, and the algebra of conditional promises, and it is still enough to sort the tools.

Terraform: diffing files against files

Terraform’s agent (the plan/apply cycle) operates on two inputs: your .tf files and a state file. The state file is a snapshot of what Terraform last saw, or more precisely, what it last wrote. terraform plan diffs one file against another file. It does not observe your infrastructure.

Between applies, Terraform has no awareness. If someone adds a security group rule through the console, Terraform does not detect it until a human runs terraform plan. If a Lambda configuration drifts, Terraform does not converge toward the desired state. It sits inert until invoked.

This fails all three properties:

  • Observation: Terraform does not observe. It reads a cached state file that another apply produced. The refresh operation partially mitigates this, but it runs only when a human invokes the tool. Between invocations, Terraform is blind. Solve that with sub-minute reconciliation loops and you have built something like Kubernetes. The state file records Terraform’s own last write, the one piece of evidence an agent assessing its own promise-keeping cannot use.

  • Local reasoning: Terraform does not reason. It diffs two data structures (desired vs. last-known) and produces a list of API calls. The reasoning was pre-computed by the human who wrote the HCL. Terraform executes; it does not decide.

  • Voluntary commitment: Terraform does not promise its own behavior; it imposes changes on remote resources through API calls. The resources promise nothing back, and Terraform promises nothing about ongoing maintenance. It applies once and stops.

Terraform’s actual model is closer to a batch script with a diffing preamble. Undeniably useful, and not what Burgess described.

Ansible: imposition from a center

Ansible’s default mode inverts promise theory. A control node connects to targets via SSH and pushes tasks. The target node has no agent, no local reasoning, no capacity to self-assess. It receives instructions and executes them.

When the control node is down, nothing converges. Connectivity that fails mid-run leaves operations partial with no mechanism to resume, and state that drifts between playbook runs goes undetected.

Against the three properties:

  • Observation: The setup module runs on the target, so the target does observe itself. It has no authority over the result. Facts travel back to the control node, when: conditions and Jinja templates evaluate there, and the decision returns as a task to execute. Observation without decision rights is telemetry rather than perception.

  • Local reasoning: Absent. The target executes tasks in the order received. It does not decide whether the task is relevant, whether the action is necessary given current state, or whether a better path exists. It runs what it was told.

  • Voluntary commitment: Inverted. The control node imposes obligations and the target makes no promise. In Burgess’s terms this is an imposition model rather than a promise model, a distinction the theory is built on.

Ansible’s actual model is remote procedure execution with YAML serialization. The “agentless” marketing is technically true (no daemon on the target) and theoretically catastrophic (no autonomous agent means no local reasoning, no convergence, no promises).

The honest exceptions

Ansible solved a real problem: managing devices where you cannot install an agent. Network switches, locked-down appliances, environments where a persistent daemon is politically or technically impossible. For those use cases, imposition is the only available mode.

ansible-pull is the second exception. Run it from cron on the target and you get a local agent that clones a playbook repository, evaluates conditions locally, and converges on a schedule with no controller involved. That is the promise-theoretic mode, shipped in the box, and almost nobody deploys it. So the critique lands on how Ansible is operated rather than on what it can do. Its dominant mode is structurally incompatible with the theory it gets associated with, and that incompatibility costs convergence, verifiability, and autonomy.

CFEngine: the one that kept it

Burgess built the reference implementation, and it satisfies the loop. A cf-agent runs on every host on a short interval, five minutes by default. It observes local state, decides locally which of its promises are unkept, and repairs those and nothing else. No controller issues orders. A policy server publishes policy and the agent pulls what it has agreed to apply, which is voluntary cooperation in the literal sense Burgess meant. Take the control loop as the test and CFEngine passes on all three counts.

Where CFEngine stops is scope and memory. A cf-agent observes what its promises describe. Write a promise about /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the agent watches that file. Write nothing about the security group in front of the host and the agent holds no opinion, because the observation is bounded by the policy that requested it. The agent’s assessment is also a verdict rather than a record. It can tell you whether the promise is kept right now. Ask what the config looked like last Tuesday, or how many times this promise has been repaired in the last month, or which hosts drifted together, and there is no queryable answer, because promise-keeping was never stored as data.

Trust in promise theory is accumulated assessment. Accumulation needs somewhere to accumulate.

Chef and Puppet: the loop inside a declaration

Chef and Puppet inherited the pull-based agent and gave part of it back. A Chef client runs on a schedule (every 30 minutes by default), pulls its run list from a server, converges toward the declared state, and reports back. A local agent runs autonomously and decides when to converge.

But the agent cannot observe beyond what its recipes describe. A Chef resource checks whether a file exists, whether a package is installed, whether a service is running. It does not survey the broader system and form a judgment about what matters. The observation is scoped to the declaration. If you did not write a resource for it, the agent does not see it.

The reasoning is also constrained: the agent converges toward whatever the recipe says. It does not ask “is this recipe still relevant?” or “has the context changed such that this action would cause harm?” It applies the declared state mechanically.

These tools approximate promise theory within the boundaries of their declarations, inheriting CFEngine’s scope bound and adding a server dependency to it. Outside those boundaries, they are as blind as Terraform between applies.

What the agent actually needs

Promise theory describes an agent that can:

  1. Look at a live system and capture what it finds
  2. Compare what it found against what it expected (or against what existed last time)
  3. Decide whether action is needed based on that comparison
  4. Act only when the decision warrants it
  5. Record what it did and what it observed, versioned over time

Steps 1 through 4 are the control loop. Step 5 is what CFEngine left out and what the declarative generation never attempted. The gap is observational capacity and retained assessment rather than syntax or speed. Those tools could not look, so we looked for them, wrote our observations into files, and handed the files to tools that could parse but not perceive.

Swamp: observation first, action second

A model method runs against a live system:

swamp model method run my-account discover_all --json

This produces typed, versioned, schema-validated data. The agent observed. The observation is stored as an immutable snapshot carrying its provenance: the model name, id, and type, the output spec that produced it, a monotonic version, an isLatest flag, a creation timestamp, and the owning run. When a workflow drove the observation, the workflow run, job, and step names ride along too.

The next execution produces a new version. Now you can diff:

swamp data query 'modelName == "my-account" && specName == "discovery" && isLatest == true' --json

Reality at T compared against reality at T-1. No declaration file in the middle. The agent queries what exists and reasons about whether the delta warrants action.

A workflow encodes the decision logic:

jobs:
  - name: observe
    steps:
      - name: scan
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: my-account
          methodName: discover_all

  - name: evaluate
    dependsOn:
      - job: observe
        condition:
          type: succeeded
    steps:
      - name: check-drift
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: drift-state
          methodName: compute_drift

The observation step runs and the evaluation step consumes its output. A downstream step acts when drift exists, and when nothing drifted the workflow terminates without side effects. The decision happens at workflow level rather than inside each resource implementation.

How the properties map

Against the three parts of the loop:

Observation. Model methods observe live systems directly. discover_all calls AWS APIs. cert_check connects to a TLS endpoint. get_os_info shells out to read the running kernel. The observation is the agent’s own act rather than a file a human pre-computed, and that is what makes the assessment worth anything.

Local reasoning. The agent (whether human or AI) queries versioned data with CEL expressions and makes decisions. “Has this changed since baseline?” is a query. “Should I act?” is a judgment the workflow encodes. The reasoning stays local to the agent’s context: it decides from what it observed rather than from instructions pushed by a controller.

Voluntary commitment. Swamp’s remote execution runs on enrollment rather than intrusion. A worker dials out to the orchestrator, presents a scoped token, and advertises what it can do:

swamp worker connect ws://orchestrator.internal:4000 \
  --token <name>.<secret> \
  --label region=us-east --label gpu=true

The orchestrator places a step only on a worker whose target name, labels, and platform match what the step asked for. With no eligible worker the step fails fast, and nothing lets the orchestrator reach a machine that never advertised the capability. That is the promise-theoretic admission rule, where an imposition lands only against a matching promise to accept. The pool is itself observable: swamp data query 'modelType == "swamp/worker"'.

Burgess’s model asks for more than this. Workers hold no repository and no credentials; they execute method bodies dispatched from the orchestrator with every capability proxied back. A worker’s promise covers its capability rather than its state, and the reasoning stays with the operator. The loop closes around the operator’s agent, and remote machines participate as promise-keeping executors rather than as autonomous peers. That is a smaller claim than CFEngine’s per-host agent can make, and it comes with the memory CFEngine never had.

Built for the reasoning agent

That architecture only pays off if an agent can consume it, and a framework can either tolerate an LLM operator or be shaped for one. The difference shows up in small decisions repeated everywhere. Swamp is shaped for one:

  • --json is a global option on every command, so structured output is the default posture rather than a flag you remember to add.
  • Data carries a Zod schema and validates on write, so an agent receives typed fields instead of prose to scrape.
  • Queries are CEL predicates over that typed data, so an agent composes a question rather than filtering text and hoping the format held.
  • Method runs and reports emit a narrative alongside the structured payload, so one result reads correctly to a person and to a model without a second rendering pass.
  • swamp agent setup lets a repository define its own agent tool definitions, so the repo tells the agent what it can do here instead of the agent guessing from a binary’s help text.
  • swamp serve exposes model and workflow execution over a WebSocket API, so an agent drives the system without a shell in the middle.

None of that makes a model correct. It removes the layer where agents fail hardest, which is parsing, guessing, and inferring structure that was never guaranteed. What remains is the part an LLM is actually good at: reading evidence and forming a judgment about it.

A human can drive all of this by hand, and reading data queries and running workflows manually works fine. That is no longer the case the design optimizes for, and saying otherwise would be false modesty about what changed.

The practical difference for a Terraform user

If you use Terraform today, here is what changes:

TerraformSwamp
State file records last-known stateVersioned data records observed state at every snapshot
plan diffs desired vs. last-knownQueries diff reality at T vs. reality at T-1
Blind between appliesScheduled observations record reality on every run
Refresh is opt-in and synchronousObservation is the primary operation
One state file per workspaceQueryable datastore across all models and domains
HCL declares what should existMethods observe what does exist; workflows decide whether to act

The shift: you stop writing declarations that tell a blind tool what to do. You start defining observations that let the agent see for itself.

The practical difference for an Ansible user

If you use Ansible today, here is what changes:

AnsibleSwamp
Central controller pushes tasks via SSHLocal agent queries and reasons; connects only when acting
Targets have no agencyObservation data makes target state visible without a daemon
No convergence between runsScheduled workflows detect drift and can correct it
Playbook reports “last push succeeded”Data query answers “is my fleet in the desired state right now?”
Idempotency is per-moduleIdempotency is a workflow decision based on observed state
gather_facts runs at push timeObservations run on schedule and persist as versioned data

Here the shift runs from pushing obligations outward and hoping they arrive intact to observing state continuously and acting only when the observation warrants it.

The observer has an availability problem too

A workflow can carry a trigger.schedule cron expression, and swamp fires it only while swamp serve is running. Schedules missed while serve was down do not catch up on startup. So the objection I aimed at Ansible’s control node lands here as well: when the observer is down, nothing observes.

What differs is the cost of a gap. A missed Ansible push leaves an intended change unmade, unrecorded, and invisible until someone pushes again. A missed observation leaves a hole in a record that is otherwise queryable, and the next run still sees current reality and still diffs it against the last stored version. CFEngine handles this better than either by putting the interval on the host, where nothing central has to be up. Anyone who wants that property today can run the schedule from the host’s own cron and point it at a shared datastore.

Idempotency moves up

Both Terraform and Ansible require idempotency at the resource/module level. Every aws_security_group_rule must detect whether it already exists. Every Ansible module must check whether the file is already in the desired state.

When the agent can query versioned state before executing, idempotency becomes a property of the workflow’s judgment. The agent asks: “has this already been done?” It checks the latest observation. If the answer is yes, it skips. The individual method does not need convergence logic because the workflow decided not to invoke it.

Swamp spells this as a step guard, a CEL expression evaluated before the step runs. A truthy result skips the step and records the reason as guarded:

- name: create-instance
  guard: ${{ data.latest("my-instance", "resource") }}
  task:
    type: model_method
    modelIdOrName: my-instance
    methodName: create

A guard can also call a method to probe live state when stored data is not enough to decide. For a scheduled workflow, guards are the difference between converging and re-running everything every thirty minutes.

Terraform pushes idempotency down because it cannot reason at a higher level. Ansible pushes idempotency down because it has no persistent state to query. Once persistent, versioned, queryable state exists, the decision moves up to the judgment layer where it belongs.

Our thinking moves up with it

Idempotency is the easiest instance to point at and the least interesting one. The same movement runs through the whole practice. We used to hand-write the convergence check, the retry, the ordering, the drift detection, and the reconciliation, one resource at a time, because no tool could be trusted with any of it. Give an agent observed state and a way to reason over it, and all of that drops into machinery. What remains for us is the altitude above it: what should be true, what evidence would show it, what is worth acting on, and what a system is entitled to promise about itself.

That is a smaller job by volume and a larger one by consequence, and it still needs a vocabulary. Promise theory earns its keep by supplying the words for exactly the questions that survive automation. Who is the agent here? What does it observe, and can it observe that directly? What may it promise, and about whom? Where does an imposition happen, and did anything on the receiving end agree to accept it? Those questions do not resolve into YAML, and no higher-level tool retires them. They get sharper as the machinery gets more capable, because more behavior is in flight and less of it sits under anyone’s direct hand.

Where declarations still matter

Three cases require stated intent, and swamp does not pretend otherwise:

Provisioning. You cannot observe what does not exist. Creating a new VPC requires specifying what you want before reality contains it. But provisioning is a small fraction of infrastructure work. Most of the work is managing what already exists.

Compliance baselines. “All S3 buckets must have encryption enabled” is intent, not observation. That intent lives in a Zod schema or a workflow condition rather than a per-resource YAML block, and it remains a declaration.

Rollback targets. “Restore Tuesday’s state” requires knowing what Tuesday looked like. Versioned data provides this, but choosing the target version is a human decision.

In all three cases, the intent lives in method logic and schema definitions rather than in static files a blind tool reads. They remain declarations in a different medium, over a much smaller surface.

The 30-year gap

Burgess shipped an agent that observed, reasoned, and promised in 1993. The missing piece was never the infrastructure agent, which could have been built at any point in the three decades since. It was the reasoning agent, the one that can look at an observation, compare it against context nobody programmed it to anticipate, and decide whether to act.

The credit for closing that gap belongs outside infrastructure, which is worth sitting with rather than glossing. Nothing in three decades of declaration formats was converging on a reasoning agent, and no amount of further refinement in that lineage would have produced one. The capability showed up as a general one and infrastructure inherited it.

Terraform cannot supply reasoning, since a state file is memory of a past action rather than perception, and neither can Ansible, whose playbook is a script pushed from a center. CFEngine had the loop and nowhere to keep what it learned.

The promise was always about agents that observe and decide, and we finally have agents that can do both. The infrastructure layer should get out of their way.

Getting started

If you have Terraform experience, the translation is:

# Install swamp
# https://swamp.club/docs/install

# Pull an AWS observation extension
swamp extension pull @webframp/aws/adopt

# Create a model instance (like defining a provider plus backend)
swamp model create @webframp/aws/adopt my-account \
  --global-arg profile=my-profile \
  --global-arg region=us-east-1

# Observe (like terraform refresh, but the primary operation)
swamp model method run my-account discover_all

# Query what you found (no equivalent in Terraform)
swamp data query 'modelName == "my-account" && isLatest == true' --json

If you have Ansible experience:

# Pull an SSH fleet extension
swamp extension pull @swamp/ssh

# Create the fleet definition, then fill in transport and hosts
swamp model create @swamp/ssh fleet --json
swamp model edit fleet

# Observe across the fleet (like gather_facts, and the output persists)
swamp model method run fleet exec \
  --input hosts=all --input command='uname -a'

# Query across all observations
swamp data query 'modelName == "fleet" && isLatest == true' --json

The fleet definition is a declaration of where to look, and it says nothing about what should be true once you get there. That boundary is the whole argument.

Instead of writing a playbook that pushes state, you define observations that persist, version, and compose. Action follows observation, so the tool sees before it touches.

The concepts outlive the tools

The value of promise theory was never the toolchain it produced. CFEngine was one implementation. Chef and Puppet were partial ones. Terraform and Ansible were not implementations at all, whatever their marketing borrowed. Swamp is another attempt, and something will supersede it. What persists across all of them is a way to reason about administering systems, which is a different kind of asset than a product.

So the honest use of a framework this durable is to hold the concepts and let the rest go. Keep autonomy, locality of knowledge, promises over impositions, and assessment by whoever observes. Give up the state file, the playbook, the run list, the per-resource convergence check, and the reflex of declaring what should be true to a tool that cannot look. Thirty years of tooling accumulated around a genuinely good idea, and most of that accumulation was scaffolding for capabilities the tools did not have. The scaffolding was the right call at the time.

Burgess was right about what agents should do, and he proved it in 1993. What took thirty years was an agent that could reason about what it saw, and a place to keep what it learned. Both showed up at once, and neither came from the direction anyone was watching.

A downstream step acts when drift exists, and when nothing drifted the workflow terminates without side effects. The decision happens at workflow level rather than inside each resource implementation.How the properties mapAgainst the three parts of the loop:Observation. Model methods observe live systems directly. discover_all calls AWS APIs. cert_check connects to a TLS endpoint. get_os_info shells out to read the running kernel. The observation is the agent’s own act rather than a file a human pre-computed, and that is what makes the assessment worth anything.Local reasoning. The agent (whether human or AI) queries versioned data with CEL expressions and makes decisions. “Has this changed since baseline?” is a query. “Should I act?” is a judgment the workflow encodes. The reasoning stays local to the agent’s context: it decides from what it observed rather than from instructions pushed by a controller.Voluntary commitment. Swamp’s remote execution runs on enrollment rather than intrusion. A worker dials out to the orchestrator, presents a scoped token, and advertises what it can do:swamp worker connect ws://orchestrator.internal:4000 \ --token <name>.<secret> \ --label region=us-east --label gpu=true The orchestrator places a step only on a worker whose target name, labels, and platform match what the step asked for. With no eligible worker the step fails fast, and nothing lets the orchestrator reach a machine that never advertised the capability. That is the promise-theoretic admission rule, where an imposition lands only against a matching promise to accept. The pool is itself observable: swamp data query 'modelType == "swamp/worker"'.Burgess’s model asks for more than this. Workers hold no repository and no credentials; they execute method bodies dispatched from the orchestrator with every capability proxied back. A worker’s promise covers its capability rather than its state, and the reasoning stays with the operator. The loop closes around the operator’s agent, and remote machines participate as promise-keeping executors rather than as autonomous peers. That is a smaller claim than CFEngine’s per-host agent can make, and it comes with the memory CFEngine never had.Built for the reasoning agentThat architecture only pays off if an agent can consume it, and a framework can either tolerate an LLM operator or be shaped for one. The difference shows up in small decisions repeated everywhere. Swamp is shaped for one:--json is a global option on every command, so structured output is the default posture rather than a flag you remember to add.Data carries a Zod schema and validates on write, so an agent receives typed fields instead of prose to scrape.Queries are CEL predicates over that typed data, so an agent composes a question rather than filtering text and hoping the format held.Method runs and reports emit a narrative alongside the structured payload, so one result reads correctly to a person and to a model without a second rendering pass.swamp agent setup lets a repository define its own agent tool definitions, so the repo tells the agent what it can do here instead of the agent guessing from a binary’s help text.swamp serve exposes model and workflow execution over a WebSocket API, so an agent drives the system without a shell in the middle.None of that makes a model correct. It removes the layer where agents fail hardest, which is parsing, guessing, and inferring structure that was never guaranteed. What remains is the part an LLM is actually good at: reading evidence and forming a judgment about it.A human can drive all of this by hand, and reading data queries and running workflows manually works fine. That is no longer the case the design optimizes for, and saying otherwise would be false modesty about what changed.The practical difference for a Terraform userIf you use Terraform today, here is what changes:TerraformSwampState file records last-known stateVersioned data records observed state at every snapshotplan diffs desired vs. last-knownQueries diff reality at T vs. reality at T-1Blind between appliesScheduled observations record reality on every runRefresh is opt-in and synchronousObservation is the primary operationOne state file per workspaceQueryable datastore across all models and domainsHCL declares what should existMethods observe what does exist; workflows decide whether to actThe shift: you stop writing declarations that tell a blind tool what to do. You start defining observations that let the agent see for itself.The practical difference for an Ansible userIf you use Ansible today, here is what changes:AnsibleSwampCentral controller pushes tasks via SSHLocal agent queries and reasons; connects only when actingTargets have no agencyObservation data makes target state visible without a daemonNo convergence between runsScheduled workflows detect drift and can correct itPlaybook reports “last push succeeded”Data query answers “is my fleet in the desired state right now?”Idempotency is per-moduleIdempotency is a workflow decision based on observed stategather_facts runs at push timeObservations run on schedule and persist as versioned dataHere the shift runs from pushing obligations outward and hoping they arrive intact to observing state continuously and acting only when the observation warrants it.The observer has an availability problem tooA workflow can carry a trigger.schedule cron expression, and swamp fires it only while swamp serve is running. Schedules missed while serve was down do not catch up on startup. So the objection I aimed at Ansible’s control node lands here as well: when the observer is down, nothing observes.What differs is the cost of a gap. A missed Ansible push leaves an intended change unmade, unrecorded, and invisible until someone pushes again. A missed observation leaves a hole in a record that is otherwise queryable, and the next run still sees current reality and still diffs it against the last stored version. CFEngine handles this better than either by putting the interval on the host, where nothing central has to be up. Anyone who wants that property today can run the schedule from the host’s own cron and point it at a shared datastore.Idempotency moves upBoth Terraform and Ansible require idempotency at the resource/module level. Every aws_security_group_rule must detect whether it already exists. Every Ansible module must check whether the file is already in the desired state.When the agent can query versioned state before executing, idempotency becomes a property of the workflow’s judgment. The agent asks: “has this already been done?” It checks the latest observation. If the answer is yes, it skips. The individual method does not need convergence logic because the workflow decided not to invoke it.Swamp spells this as a step guard, a CEL expression evaluated before the step runs. A truthy result skips the step and records the reason as guarded:- name: create-instance guard: ${{ data.latest("my-instance", "resource") }} task: type: model_method modelIdOrName: my-instance methodName: create A guard can also call a method to probe live state when stored data is not enough to decide. For a scheduled workflow, guards are the difference between converging and re-running everything every thirty minutes.Terraform pushes idempotency down because it cannot reason at a higher level. Ansible pushes idempotency down because it has no persistent state to query. Once persistent, versioned, queryable state exists, the decision moves up to the judgment layer where it belongs.Our thinking moves up with itIdempotency is the easiest instance to point at and the least interesting one. The same movement runs through the whole practice. We used to hand-write the convergence check, the retry, the ordering, the drift detection, and the reconciliation, one resource at a time, because no tool could be trusted with any of it. Give an agent observed state and a way to reason over it, and all of that drops into machinery. What remains for us is the altitude above it: what should be true, what evidence would show it, what is worth acting on, and what a system is entitled to promise about itself.That is a smaller job by volume and a larger one by consequence, and it still needs a vocabulary. Promise theory earns its keep by supplying the words for exactly the questions that survive automation. Who is the agent here? What does it observe, and can it observe that directly? What may it promise, and about whom? Where does an imposition happen, and did anything on the receiving end agree to accept it? Those questions do not resolve into YAML, and no higher-level tool retires them. They get sharper as the machinery gets more capable, because more behavior is in flight and less of it sits under anyone’s direct hand.Where declarations still matterThree cases require stated intent, and swamp does not pretend otherwise:Provisioning. You cannot observe what does not exist. Creating a new VPC requires specifying what you want before reality contains it. But provisioning is a small fraction of infrastructure work. Most of the work is managing what already exists.Compliance baselines. “All S3 buckets must have encryption enabled” is intent, not observation. That intent lives in a Zod schema or a workflow condition rather than a per-resource YAML block, and it remains a declaration.Rollback targets. “Restore Tuesday’s state” requires knowing what Tuesday looked like. Versioned data provides this, but choosing the target version is a human decision.In all three cases, the intent lives in method logic and schema definitions rather than in static files a blind tool reads. They remain declarations in a different medium, over a much smaller surface.The 30-year gapBurgess shipped an agent that observed, reasoned, and promised in 1993. The missing piece was never the infrastructure agent, which could have been built at any point in the three decades since. It was the reasoning agent, the one that can look at an observation, compare it against context nobody programmed it to anticipate, and decide whether to act.The credit for closing that gap belongs outside infrastructure, which is worth sitting with rather than glossing. Nothing in three decades of declaration formats was converging on a reasoning agent, and no amount of further refinement in that lineage would have produced one. The capability showed up as a general one and infrastructure inherited it.Terraform cannot supply reasoning, since a state file is memory of a past action rather than perception, and neither can Ansible, whose playbook is a script pushed from a center. CFEngine had the loop and nowhere to keep what it learned.The promise was always about agents that observe and decide, and we finally have agents that can do both. The infrastructure layer should get out of their way.Getting startedIf you have Terraform experience, the translation is:# Install swamp # https://swamp.club/docs/install # Pull an AWS observation extension swamp extension pull @webframp/aws/adopt # Create a model instance (like defining a provider plus backend) swamp model create @webframp/aws/adopt my-account \ --global-arg profile=my-profile \ --global-arg region=us-east-1 # Observe (like terraform refresh, but the primary operation) swamp model method run my-account discover_all # Query what you found (no equivalent in Terraform) swamp data query 'modelName == "my-account" && isLatest == true' --json If you have Ansible experience:# Pull an SSH fleet extension swamp extension pull @swamp/ssh # Create the fleet definition, then fill in transport and hosts swamp model create @swamp/ssh fleet --json swamp model edit fleet # Observe across the fleet (like gather_facts, and the output persists) swamp model method run fleet exec \ --input hosts=all --input command='uname -a' # Query across all observations swamp data query 'modelName == "fleet" && isLatest == true' --json The fleet definition is a declaration of where to look, and it says nothing about what should be true once you get there. That boundary is the whole argument.Instead of writing a playbook that pushes state, you define observations that persist, version, and compose. Action follows observation, so the tool sees before it touches.The concepts outlive the toolsThe value of promise theory was never the toolchain it produced. CFEngine was one implementation. Chef and Puppet were partial ones. Terraform and Ansible were not implementations at all, whatever their marketing borrowed. Swamp is another attempt, and something will supersede it. What persists across all of them is a way to reason about administering systems, which is a different kind of asset than a product.So the honest use of a framework this durable is to hold the concepts and let the rest go. Keep autonomy, locality of knowledge, promises over impositions, and assessment by whoever observes. Give up the state file, the playbook, the run list, the per-resource convergence check, and the reflex of declaring what should be true to a tool that cannot look. Thirty years of tooling accumulated around a genuinely good idea, and most of that accumulation was scaffolding for capabilities the tools did not have. The scaffolding was the right call at the time.Burgess was right about what agents should do, and he proved it in 1993. What took thirty years was an agent that could reason about what it saw, and a place to keep what it learned. Both showed up at once, and neither came from the direction anyone was watching.

blocks.html_en: Mark Burgess shipped CFEngine in 1993, formalized promise theory with Siri Fagernes around 2005, and published In Search of Certainty in 2015. The model is precise: autonomous agents observe their environment, reason locally about what they find, and make promises about their own behavior. The agent does not receive instructions from a controller. The agent looks around, decides what to do, and commits to doing it.

blocks.html_en: Ansible’s default mode inverts promise theory. A control node connects to targets via SSH and pushes tasks. The target node has no agent, no local reasoning, no capacity to self-assess. It receives instructions and executes them.

sentences.en: Ansible’s default mode inverts promise theory.
sentences.zh: Ansible 的默认模式颠倒了承诺理论。

sentences.en: A control node connects to targets via SSH and pushes tasks.
sentences.zh: 控制节点通过 SSH 连接到目标并推送任务。

sentences.en: The target node has no agent, no local reasoning, no capacity to self-assess.

sentences.en: It receives instructions and executes them.
sentences.zh: 它接收指令并执行它们。

blocks.html_en: The honest exceptions

sentences.en: The honest exceptions
sentences.zh: 诚实的例外

blocks.html_en: Ansible solved a real problem: managing devices where you cannot install an agent. Network switches, locked-down appliances, environments where a persistent daemon is politically or technically impossible. For those use cases, imposition is the only available mode.

sentences.en: Ansible solved a real problem: managing devices where you cannot install an agent.
sentences.zh: Ansible 解决了一个真正的问题：管理无法安装代理的设备。

sentences.en: Network switches, locked-down appliances, environments where a persistent daemon is politically or technically impossible.

blocks.html_en: ansible-pull is the second exception. blocks.html_en: CFEngine: the one that kept it

sentences.en: CFEngine: the one that kept it
sentences.zh: CFEngine：保留它的那个

blocks.html_en: Burgess built the reference implementation, and it satisfies the loop. A cf-agent runs on every host on a short interval, five minutes by default. It observes local state, decides locally which of its promises are unkept, and repairs those and nothing else. No controller issues orders. A policy server publishes policy and the agent pulls what it has agreed to apply, which is voluntary cooperation in the literal sense Burgess meant. Take the control loop as the test and CFEngine passes on all three counts.

sentences.en: Burgess built the reference implementation, and it satisfies the loop.
sentences.zh: Burgess 构建了参考实现，它满足循环。

sentences.en: A cf-agent runs on every host on a short interval, five minutes by default.
sentences.zh: cf-agent 在每个主机上运行的时间间隔很短，默认情况下为五分钟。

sentences.en: It observes local state, decides locally which of its promises are unkept, and repairs those and nothing else.
sentences.zh: 它观察当地的状态，在当地决定哪些承诺没有兑现，并修复这些承诺，而不是其他。

sentences.en: No controller issues orders.
sentences.zh: 没有管制员发出命令。

sentences.en: A policy server publishes policy and the agent pulls what it has agreed to apply, which is voluntary cooperation in the literal sense Burgess meant.
sentences.zh: 策略服务器发布策略，代理提取其同意应用的内容，这就是伯吉斯字面意义上的自愿合作。

sentences.en: Take the control loop as the test and CFEngine passes on all three counts.
sentences.zh: 以控制循环作为测试，CFEngine 通过了所有三个指标。

blocks.html_en: Where CFEngine stops is scope and memory. A cf-agent observes what its promises describe. Write a promise about /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the agent watches that file. Write nothing about the security group in front of the host and the agent holds no opinion, because the observation is bounded by the policy that requested it. The agent’s assessment is also a verdict rather than a record. It can tell you whether the promise is kept right now. Ask what the config looked like last Tuesday, or how many times this promise has been repaired in the last month, or which hosts drifted together, and there is no queryable answer, because promise-keeping was never stored as data.

sentences.en: Where CFEngine stops is scope and memory.
sentences.zh: CFEngine 停止的地方是作用域和内存。

sentences.en: Write a promise about /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the agent watches that file.
sentences.zh: 写一个关于 /etc/ssh/sshd_config 的承诺，代理会监视该文件。

sentences.en: Write nothing about the security group in front of the host and the agent holds no opinion, because the observation is bounded by the policy that requested it.
sentences.zh: 在主机面前不写任何有关安全组的内容，代理也不持有任何意见，因为观察受到请求它的策略的限制。

sentences.en: The agent’s assessment is also a verdict rather than a record.
sentences.zh: 代理人的评估也是一个判决而不是一个记录。

sentences.en: It can tell you whether the promise is kept right now.
sentences.zh: 它可以告诉您现在是否兑现了承诺。

sentences.en: Ask what the config looked like last Tuesday, or how many times this promise has been repaired in the last month, or which hosts drifted together, and there is no queryable answer, because promise-keeping was never stored as data.
sentences.zh: 询问上周二的配置是什么样子，或者这个承诺在上个月被修复了多少次，或者哪些主机漂移在一起，并且没有可查询的答案，因为承诺从未被存储为数据。

blocks.html_en: Trust in promise theory is accumulated assessment. Accumulation needs somewhere to accumulate.

sentences.en: Trust in promise theory is accumulated assessment.
sentences.zh: 对承诺理论的信任是累积的评估。

sentences.en: Accumulation needs somewhere to accumulate.
sentences.zh: 积累需要有积累的地方。

blocks.html_en: Chef and Puppet: the loop inside a declaration

sentences.en: Chef and Puppet: the loop inside a declaration
sentences.zh: Chef 和 Puppet：声明内的循环

blocks.html_en: Chef and Puppet inherited the pull-based agent and gave part of it back. A Chef client runs on a schedule (every 30 minutes by default), pulls its run list from a server, converges toward the declared state, and reports back. A local agent runs autonomously and decides when to converge.

sentences.en: Chef and Puppet inherited the pull-based agent and gave part of it back.
sentences.zh: Chef和Puppet继承了基于拉动的代理并返还了一部分。

sentences.en: A Chef client runs on a schedule (every 30 minutes by default), pulls its run list from a server, converges toward the declared state, and reports back.
sentences.zh: Chef 客户端按计划运行（默认情况下每 30 分钟一次），从服务器提取其运行列表，收敛到声明的状态，然后返回报告。

sentences.en: A local agent runs autonomously and decides when to converge.
sentences.zh: 本地代理自主运行并决定何时收敛。

blocks.html_en: But the agent cannot observe beyond what its recipes describe. A Chef resource checks whether a file exists, whether a package is installed, whether a service is running. It does not survey the broader system and form a judgment about what matters. The observation is scoped to the declaration. If you did not write a resource for it, the agent does not see it.

sentences.en: But the agent cannot observe beyond what its recipes describe.
sentences.zh: 但代理无法观察超出其配方描述的内容。

sentences.en: A Chef resource checks whether a file exists, whether a package is installed, whether a service is running.
sentences.zh: Chef 资源检查文件是否存在、软件包是否安装、服务是否正在运行。

sentences.en: It does not survey the broader system and form a judgment about what matters.
sentences.zh: 它不会调查更广泛的系统并对重要的事情形成判断。

sentences.en: The observation is scoped to the declaration.
sentences.zh: 观察范围仅限于声明。

sentences.en: If you did not write a resource for it, the agent does not see it.
sentences.zh: 如果您没有为其编写资源，代理就看不到它。

blocks.html_en: The reasoning is also constrained: the agent converges toward whatever the recipe says. It does not ask “is this recipe still relevant?” or “has the context changed such that this action would cause harm?” It applies the declared state mechanically.

sentences.en: The reasoning is also constrained: the agent converges toward whatever the recipe says.
sentences.zh: 推理也受到限制：智能体会趋向于配方所说的任何内容。

sentences.en: It does not ask “is this recipe still relevant?”
sentences.zh: 它不会问“这个食谱仍然相关吗？”

sentences.zh: 或者“环境是否发生变化，导致该行为会造成伤害？”

sentences.en: It applies the declared state mechanically.
sentences.zh: 它机械地应用声明的状态。

blocks.html_en: These tools approximate promise theory within the boundaries of their declarations, inheriting CFEngine’s scope bound and adding a server dependency to it. Outside those boundaries, they are as blind as Terraform between applies.

sentences.en: These tools approximate promise theory within the boundaries of their declarations, inheriting CFEngine’s scope bound and adding a server dependency to it.

blocks.html_en: What the agent actually needs

sentences.en: What the agent actually needs
sentences.zh: 代理实际需要什么

blocks.html_en: Promise theory describes an agent that can:

sentences.en: Promise theory describes an agent that can:
sentences.zh: 承诺理论描述了一个代理可以：

blocks.html_en: • Look at a live system and capture what it finds

sentences.en: Look at a live system and capture what it finds

blocks.html_en: • Compare what it found against what it expected (or against what existed last time)

blocks.html_en: Steps 1 through 4 are the control loop. Step 5 is what CFEngine left out and what the declarative generation never attempted. The gap is observational capacity and retained assessment rather than syntax or speed. Those tools could not look, so we looked for them, wrote our observations into files, and handed the files to tools that could parse but not perceive.

sentences.zh: 第 5 步是 CFEngine 遗漏的部分，也是声明式生成从未尝试过的部分。

sentences.en: The gap is observational capacity and retained assessment rather than syntax or speed.

sentences.en: Those tools could not look, so we looked for them, wrote our observations into files, and handed the files to tools that could parse but not perceive.

content_html_zh:
Mark Burgess 于 1993 年推出了 CFEngine，在 2005 年左右与 Siri Fagernes 一起将承诺理论正式化，并于 2015 年出版了《寻找确定性》。 该模型是精确的：自主代理观察他们的环境，对他们发现的情况进行本地推理，并对自己的行为做出承诺。 代理不接收来自控制器的指令。 代理人环顾四周，决定做什么，并承诺去做。

此后的每一个基础设施工具都继承了这个想法。 Chef 称其资源“聚合”。 Puppet 将其目录称为“理想状态”。 Terraform 称其计划是“声明性的”。 Ansible 称其剧本为“幂等”。

这四个人都没有遵守诺言。 伯吉斯自己的工具做到了，但遇到了不同的限制。

现在重新审视这一切的原因是，缺失的部分终于发货了，而且它完全是从外部基础设施到达的。 法学硕士提供了始终假设的推理层承诺理论：代理可以观察实时系统，根据没有事先列举的上下文来权衡它所发现的内容，并决定是否采取行动。 四代工具无论付出什么代价都无法做到这一点。 CFEngine 最接近，但由于值得精确说明的原因而停止了，而 swamp 是为可以做到这一点的代理而构建的。

承诺理论控制循环

承诺理论从三个公理开始。 代理人是自主的，不能被强迫。 代理人只能承诺自己的行为。 代理人对世界的了解是本地的。 将它们组合起来，你就得到了一个控制循环：

  1. 观察。 代理直接感知其环境。 不是来自文件。 不是来自其他人制作的状态快照。 经纪人看着。 知识是局部的，因此不存在全局观察者来向代理提供摘要，而承诺是由观察者评估的，因此代理自己没有做出的评估不会给它带来任何好处。
  2. 局部推理。 代理根据观察到的情况决定做什么。 没有中央控制器指示操作。 代理人的判断在其管辖范围内具有主权。
  3. 自愿承诺。 代理承诺自己的行为。 它不会将行为强加于他人。 承诺是您对自己做出的承诺，而不是您强加给远程系统的义务。 收款代理人从未承诺接受的强制措施不会有任何效果。

观察、推理、承诺。 该循环遗漏了大部分承诺理论，包括信任积累、合作均衡和条件承诺代数，但对工具进行排序仍然足够了。

Terraform：比较文件与文件

Terraform 的代理（计划/应用周期）对两个输入进行操作：您的 .tf 文件和状态文件。 状态文件是 Terraform 最后看到的内容的快照，或者更准确地说，是它最后写入的内容的快照。 terraform plan 将一个文件与另一个文件进行比较。 它不会观察您的基础设施。

在应用之间，Terraform 没有意识。 如果有人通过控制台添加安全组规则，Terraform 不会检测到它，直到有人运行 terraform 计划。 如果 Lambda 配置发生漂移，Terraform 不会收敛到所需状态。 在被调用之前它是惰性的。

这三个属性都失败了：

  • 观察：Terraform 不观察。 它读取另一个应用程序生成的缓存状态文件。 刷新操作部分缓解了这种情况，但它仅在人类调用该工具时运行。 在调用之间，Terraform 是盲目的。 通过亚分钟协调循环解决这个问题，您就构建了类似 Kubernetes 的东西。 状态文件记录了 Terraform 自己的最后一次写入，这是评估其自身承诺履行情况的代理无法使用的唯一证据。
  • 本地推理：Terraform 不推理。 它区分两种数据结构（所需的与最后已知的）并生成 API 调用列表。 推理是由编写 HCL 的人预先计算的。 Terraform 执行；它并不能决定。
  • 自愿承诺：Terraform 不承诺自身行为；它通过 API 调用对远程资源进行更改。 资源不承诺任何回报，Terraform 也不承诺持续维护。 它适用一次并停止。

Terraform 的实际模型更接近于带有差异前导码的批处理脚本。 不可否认有用，但不是伯吉斯所描述的那样。

Ansible：从中心强加

Ansible 的默认模式颠倒了承诺理论。 控制节点通过 SSH 连接到目标并推送任务。 目标节点没有代理，没有本地推理，没有自我评估的能力。 它接收指令并执行它们。

当控制节点关闭时，没有任何收敛。 运行中失败的连接会使部分操作无法恢复，并且在 playbook 运行之间漂移的状态不会被检测到。

针对三个属性：

  • 观察：设置模块在目标上运行，因此目标会观察自身。 它对结果没有权力。 事实返回到控制节点，此时： 条件和 Jinja 模板在那里进行评估，并且决策作为要执行的任务返回。 没有决策权的观察是遥测而不是感知。
  • 局部推理：不存在。 目标按照收到的顺序执行任务。 它不会决定任务是否相关，在当前状态下是否有必要采取行动，或者是否存在更好的路径。 它按照指令运行。
  • 自愿承诺：倒置。 控制节点施加义务，目标不做出承诺。 用伯吉斯的话说，这是一种强加模型，而不是承诺模型，这是该理论建立的基础上的区别。

Ansible 的实际模型是使用 YAML 序列化的远程过程执行。 “无代理”营销在技术上是正确的（目标上没有守护进程），但在理论上是灾难性的（没有自主代理意味着没有本地推理、没有收敛、没有承诺）。

诚实的例外

Ansible 解决了一个真正的问题：管理无法安装代理的设备。 网络交换机、锁定设备、持久守护进程在政治上或技术上不可能的环境。 对于这些用例，拼版是唯一可用的模式。

ansible-pull 是第二个例外。 从目标上的 cron 运行它，您将获得一个本地代理，该代理克隆 playbook 存储库、在本地评估条件并按计划收敛，而无需涉及控制器。 这就是承诺理论模式，随盒装运，几乎没有人部署它。 因此，批评集中在 Ansible 的运作方式上，而不是它能做什么。 它的主导模式在结构上与其相关的理论不相容，并且这种不相容性会导致收敛性、可验证性和自主性的代价。

CFEngine：保留它的那个

Burgess 构建了参考实现，它满足循环。 cf-agent 在每个主机上运行的时间间隔很短，默认情况下为五分钟。 它观察当地的状态，在当地决定哪些承诺没有兑现，并修复这些承诺，而不是其他。 没有管制员发出命令。 策略服务器发布策略，代理提取其同意应用的内容，这就是伯吉斯字面意义上的自愿合作。 以控制循环作为测试，CFEngine 通过了所有三个指标。

CFEngine 停止的地方是作用域和内存。 cf-agent 观察其承诺所描述的内容。 写一个关于 /etc/ssh/sshd_config 的承诺，代理会监视该文件。 在主机面前不写任何有关安全组的内容，代理也不持有任何意见，因为观察受到请求它的策略的限制。 代理人的评估也是一个判决而不是一个记录。 它可以告诉您现在是否兑现了承诺。 询问上周二的配置是什么样子，或者这个承诺在上个月被修复了多少次，或者哪些主机漂移在一起，并且没有可查询的答案，因为承诺从未被存储为数据。

对承诺理论的信任是累积的评估。 积累需要有积累的地方。

Chef 和 Puppet：声明内的循环

Chef和Puppet继承了基于拉动的代理并返还了一部分。 Chef 客户端按计划运行（默认情况下每 30 分钟一次），从服务器提取其运行列表，收敛到声明的状态，然后返回报告。 本地代理自主运行并决定何时收敛。

但代理无法观察超出其配方描述的内容。 Chef 资源检查文件是否存在、软件包是否安装、服务是否正在运行。 它不会调查更广泛的系统并对重要的事情形成判断。 观察范围仅限于声明。 如果您没有为其编写资源，代理就看不到它。

推理也受到限制：智能体会趋向于配方所说的任何内容。 它不会问“这个食谱仍然相关吗？” 或者“环境是否发生变化，导致该行为会造成伤害？” 它机械地应用声明的状态。

这些工具在其声明的范围内近似承诺理论，继承 CFEngine 的范围界限并向其添加服务器依赖项。 在这些边界之外，它们就像 Terraform 之间的应用一样盲目。

代理实际需要什么

承诺理论描述了一个代理可以：

  1. 查看实时系统并捕获它所发现的内容
  2. 将发现的内容与预期的内容（或上次存在的内容）进行比较
  3. 根据比较结果决定是否需要采取行动
  4. 仅在决策需要时才采取行动
  5. 记录它做了什么和观察到了什么，并随着时间的推移进行版本化

步骤 1 到 4 是控制循环。 第 5 步是 CFEngine 遗漏的部分，也是声明式生成从未尝试过的部分。 差距在于观察能力和保留评估能力，而不是语法或速度。 这些工具看不到，所以我们寻找它们，将我们的观察写入文件，并将文件交给可以解析但不能感知的工具。

沼泽：观察第一，行动第二

模型方法针对实时系统运行：

swamp model method run my-account discover_all --json

这会生成类型化、版本化、模式验证的数据。 代理人观察到。 观察结果存储为不可变的快照，其中包含其出处：模型名称、id 和类型、生成它的输出规范、单调版本、isLatest 标志、创建时间戳和所属运行。 当工作流驱动观察时，工作流运行、作业和步骤名称也会随之变化。

下一次执行会产生一个新版本。 现在你可以比较：

swamp data query 'modelName == "my-account" && specName == "discovery" && isLatest == true' --json

T 处的现实与 T-1 处的现实进行比较。 中间没有声明文件。 代理查询存在的内容以及增量是否值得采取行动的原因。

工作流程对决策逻辑进行编码：

jobs:
  - name: observe
    steps:
      - name: scan
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: my-account
          methodName: discover_all

  - name: evaluate
    dependsOn:
      - job: observe
        condition:
          type: succeeded
    steps:
      - name: check-drift
        task:
          type: model_method
          modelIdOrName: drift-state
          methodName: compute_drift

观察步骤运行，评估步骤消耗其输出。 当存在漂移时，下游步骤将起作用，并且当没有任何漂移时，工作流将终止，而不会产生副作用。 该决策发生在工作流级别，而不是在每个资源实现内部。

属性如何映射

针对循环的三个部分：

观察。 模型方法直接观察实时系统。 discovery_all 调用 AWS API。 cert_check 连接到 TLS 端点。 get_os_info shell 读取正在运行的内核。 观察结果是智能体自己的行为，而不是人类预先计算的文件，这就是评估有价值的原因。

局部推理。 代理（无论是人类还是人工智能）使用 CEL 表达式查询版本化数据并做出决策。 “自基线以来，情况有变化吗？” 是一个查询。 “我应该行动吗？” 是工作流编码的判断。 推理保持在代理的上下文中：它根据观察到的内容而不是控制器推送的指令来决定。

自愿承诺。 Swamp 的远程执行基于注册而不是入侵。 工作人员拨出编排器，提供范围令牌，并宣传它可以做什么：

swamp worker connect ws://orchestrator.internal:4000 \
  --token <name>.<secret> \
  --label region=us-east --label gpu=true

协调器仅将步骤放置在目标名称、标签和平台与步骤要求匹配的工作人员上。 如果没有合格的工作人员，该步骤很快就会失败，并且编排器无法到达从未公布过该功能的机器。 这就是承诺理论的准入规则，只有在匹配的承诺接受的情况下，强制才会生效。 池本身是可观察的：沼泽数据查询'modelType ==“swamp/worker”'。

伯吉斯的模型要求的不仅仅是这个。 工作人员没有存储库，也没有凭证；他们执行从编排器分派的方法体，并代理返回每个功能。 工人的承诺涵盖其能力而不是其状态，并且推理取决于操作员。 该循环围绕操作员的代理闭合，远程机器作为信守诺言的执行者而不是作为自治对等点参与。 这比 CFEngine 的每主机代理所能提出的要求要小，而且它配备了 CFEngine 从未有过的内存。

为推理代理而构建

只有当代理可以使用该架构，并且框架可以容忍 LLM 操作员或为 LLM 操作员而设计时，该架构才能获得回报。 差异体现在各处重复的小决定中。 沼泽的形状为一：

  • --json 是每个命令的全局选项，因此结构化输出是默认姿势，而不是您记得添加的标志。
  • 数据带有 Zod 模式并在写入时进行验证，因此代理会接收键入的字段而不是要抓取的散文。
  • 查询是针对键入的数据的 CEL 谓词，因此代理会提出问题，而不是过滤文本并希望保留格式。
  • 方法运行和报告会在结构化负载旁边发出叙述，因此人员和模型可以正确读取一个结果，而无需第二次渲染过程。
  • 沼泽代理设置允许存储库定义自己的代理工具定义，因此存储库告诉代理它可以在这里做什么，而不是代理从二进制文件的帮助文本中猜测。
  • swamp 服务通过 WebSocket API 公开模型和工作流执行，因此代理可以驱动系统，而无需中间的 shell。

这些都不能保证模型正确。 它消除了代理最难失败的一层，即解析、猜测和推断从未得到保证的结构。 剩下的就是法学硕士真正擅长的部分：阅读证据并对其做出判断。

人类可以手动驱动所有这些，并且手动读取数据查询和运行工作流程效果很好。 设计优化的情况不再是这样，否则的话就是对变化的虚伪谦虚。

Terraform 用户的实际差异

如果您现在使用 Terraform，则会发生以下变化：

地形Swamp
状态文件记录最后已知的状态版本化数据记录每个快照观察到的状态
期望计划与最后已知计划的差异查询 T 处的现实与 T-1 处的现实的差异
申请之间盲目预定的观察记录每次运行的现实
刷新是选择加入且同步的观察是首要操作
每个工作区一个状态文件跨所有模型和域的可查询数据存储
HCL 声明什么应该存在方法观察存在的事物；工作流程决定是否采取行动

转变：您不再编写告诉盲目工具要做什么的声明。 您开始定义观察结果，让智能体亲眼目睹。

Ansible 用户的实际差异

如果您现在使用 Ansible，则会发生以下变化：

安西布尔Swamp
中央控制器通过SSH推送任务当地代理查询及原因；仅在动作时连接
目标没有代理机构观察数据使目标状态可见，无需守护程序
运行之间没有收敛预定的工作流程检测偏差并可以纠正它
Playbook 报告“上次推送成功”数据查询回答“我的车队现在处于期望的状态吗？”

Gather_facts 在推送时运行观察按计划运行并保留为版本数据

这里的转变是从将义务向外推并希望它们完好无损地到达，到持续观察状态并仅在观察到的情况下才采取行动。

观察者也存在可用性问题

工作流可以携带trigger.schedule cron表达式，并且swamp仅在s​​wamp服务运行时触发它。 服务中断时错过的时间表无法赶上启动时间。 所以我针对 Ansible 控制节点的反对意见也在这里：当观察者宕机时，什么也观察不到。

不同之处在于缺口的成本。 错过 Ansible 推送会导致预期的更改未完成、未记录且不可见，直到有人再次推送为止。 错过的观察会在记录中留下一个可查询的漏洞，并且下一次运行仍然会看到当前的现实，并且仍然将其与最后存储的版本进行比较。 CFEngine 比将间隔放在主机上更好地处理这个问题，而主机上不需要启动任何中央设备。 今天任何想要该属性的人都可以从主机自己的 cron 运行计划并将其指向共享数据存储。

幂等性上升

Terraform 和 Ansible 都需要资源/模块级别的幂等性。 每个 aws_security_group_rule 必须检测它是否已存在。 每个 Ansible 模块都必须检查文件是否已处于所需状态。

当代理可以在执行之前查询版本化状态时，幂等性就成为工作流判断的一个属性。 代理人问：“这已经完成了吗？” 它检查最新的观察结果。 如果答案是肯定的，则会跳过。 单个方法不需要收敛逻辑，因为工作流决定不调用它。

Swamp 将其拼写为步骤防护，是在步骤运行之前评估的 CEL 表达式。 真实的结果会跳过该步骤并将原因记录为受保护：

- name: create-instance
  guard: ${{ data.latest("my-instance", "resource") }}
  task:
    type: model_method
    modelIdOrName: my-instance
    methodName: create

当存储的数据不足以做出决定时，警卫还可以调用方法来探测实时状态。 对于预定的工作流程，警卫是每三十分钟收敛和重新运行所有内容之间的区别。

Terraform 降低了幂等性，因为它无法在更高级别进行推理。 Ansible 降低了幂等性，因为它没有持久状态可供查询。 一旦持久的、版本化的、可查询的状态存在，决策就会上升到它所属的判断层。

我们的思想随之进步

幂等性是最容易指出的例子，也是最无趣的例子。 同一个动作贯穿整个练习过程。 我们过去常常手写收敛检查、重试、排序、偏差检测和协调，一次一个资源，因为没有任何工具可以信任其中的任何一个。 给智能体观察到的状态以及对其进行推理的方法，所有这些都会落入机器中。 我们剩下的就是高于它的高度：什么应该是真实的，什么证据可以证明它，什么值得采取行动，以及一个系统有权对自己做出什么承诺。

从体积上看，这是一项较小的工作，但从结果上看，这是一项较大的工作，而且它仍然需要词汇表。 承诺理论通过为自动化中幸存的问题提供准确的词语而得以生存。 这里的代理是谁？ 它观察到什么？它可以直接观察到吗？ 它可以许诺什么，又许诺给谁？ 强加是在哪里发生的，接收端是否同意接受它？ 这些问题不会在 YAML 中得到解决，也没有更高级别的工具可以淘汰它们。 随着机器的能力变得更强，它们也会变得更加敏锐，因为更多的行为是在飞行中发生的，而受到任何人直接控制的行为则越来越少。

声明仍然重要的地方

三种情况需要表明意图，swamp 不会假装不这样做：

供应。 你无法观察不存在的事物。 创建新的 VPC 需要在现实包含它之前指定您想要的内容。 但配置只是基础设施工作的一小部分。 大部分工作是管理已经存在的东西。

合规基线。 “所有 S3 存储桶必须启用加密”是意图，而不是观察。 该意图存在于 Zod 模式或工作流条件中，而不是每个资源的 YAML 块中，并且它仍然是一个声明。

回滚目标。 “恢复星期二的状态”需要知道星期二是什么样子。 版本化数据提供了这一点，但选择目标版本是人类的决定。

在所有三种情况下，意图都存在于方法逻辑和模式定义中，而不是盲工具读取的静态文件中。 它们仍然是在不同媒介、更小的表面上的声明。

30年的差距

伯吉斯在 1993 年派遣了一名观察、推理和承诺的代理人。 缺失的部分从来都不是基础设施代理，它可以在此后三十年的任何时候建立。 它是推理代理，可以查看观察结果，将其与无人编程预测的上下文进行比较，并决定是否采取行动。

缩小这一差距的功劳属于基础设施之外，值得坐视而不是掩饰。 在三十年的声明格式中，没有任何东西能够汇聚到推理代理上，并且对该谱系进行再多的进一步细化也不会产生推理代理。 该功能表现为通用功能，基础设施继承了它。

Terraform 无法提供推理，因为状态文件是过去动作的记忆，而不是感知，Ansible 也不能提供推理，它的剧本是从中心推送的脚本。 CFEngine 有循环，但无处保存它学到的东西。

我们的承诺始终是关于观察和决策的代理，而我们终于拥有了可以同时做到这两点的代理。 基础设施层应该让路。

入门

如果您有 Terraform 经验，则翻译为：

# Install swamp
# https://swamp.club/docs/install

# Pull an AWS observation extension
swamp extension pull @webframp/aws/adopt

# Create a model instance (like defining a provider plus backend)
swamp model create @webframp/aws/adopt my-account \
  --global-arg profile=my-profile \
  --global-arg region=us-east-1

# Observe (like terraform refresh, but the primary operation)
swamp model method run my-account discover_all

# Query what you found (no equivalent in Terraform)
swamp data query 'modelName == "my-account" && isLatest == true' --json

如果您有 Ansible 经验：

# Pull an SSH fleet extension
swamp extension pull @swamp/ssh

# Create the fleet definition, then fill in transport and hosts
swamp model create @swamp/ssh fleet --json
swamp model edit fleet

# Observe across the fleet (like gather_facts, and the output persists)
swamp model method run fleet exec \
  --input hosts=all --input command='uname -a'

# Query across all observations
swamp data query 'modelName == "fleet" && isLatest == true' --json

机队定义是对去哪里寻找的声明，它没有说明到达那里后应该发生什么。 这个边界就是整个论证。

您无需编写推动状态的剧本，而是定义持久、版本和组合的观察。 观察之后采取行动，因此该工具在接触之前先看到。

概念比工具更长久

承诺理论的价值从来不在于它产生的工具链。 CFEngine 是一种实现。 Chef和Puppet是偏心的。 无论 Terraform 和 Ansible 的营销手段如何，它们根本就不是实现。 沼泽是另一种尝试，有些东西会取代它。 所有这些都坚持一种管理系统的推理方式，这是一种与产品不同的资产。

因此，诚实地使用一个如此持久的框架就是保留概念并放弃其余的。 保持自主权、知识本地化、承诺而非强制以及由观察者进行评估。 放弃状态文件、剧本、运行列表、每个资源的收敛检查，以及对无法查看的工具声明什么应该是真实的反射。 三十年的工具围绕着一个真正的好主意积累起来，其中大部分积累都是为工具所不具备的功能搭建的脚手架。 脚手架在当时是正确的选择。

伯吉斯对于特工应该做什么的看法是正确的，他在 1993 年证明了这一点。 花了三十年的时间才得到一个能够推理它所看到的东西的智能体，以及一个保存它所学到的东西的地方。 两人同时出现，而且都不是来自众人注视的方向。
